newsitem.title: FRANCE: Egypt director preaches tolerance after film ban.
newsitem.headline: Egypt director preaches tolerance after film ban.

text.p: Veteran Youssef Chahine, whose last film "The Migrant" was banned in Egypt, has answered his Moslem fundamentalist censors with an ode to tolerance screened in competition at the Cannes festival on Thursday.

The 72-year-old Egyptian director, who first appeared in Cannes at the age of 24 with "The Son of the Nile", chronicles in "Al Massir" (The Destiny) the trials of the 12th century philosopher Averroes who lived in Moslem Spain.
A Franco-Egyptian co-production shot in Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and France, it mirrors Chahine's own ordeal as Averroes' books were ordered burned after a protest by religious fundamentalists.
"Through the philosopher's story, my film urges tolerance. If it existed in Andalusia in the golden age of Islam, why shouldn't the same be true today," Chahine said.

Asked about parallels with his own career, he said: "When I was threatened, people wanted to impose bodyguards on me. I refused and instead of locking myself up, I went out into the street. I was safe there, because the man in the street has always understood me better than the authorities."

His previous film was banned in 1995 after fundamentalists said it resembled the story of the patriarch Joseph, in violation of the orthodox Islamic view those whom Moslmes consider prophets cannot be portrayed or impersonated.

Chahine's lawyers argued that the plot of the film, which was seen by at least two million people before it was banned, differed from the story of Joseph as it appears in the Koran and so the question of depicting a prophet did not arise.

Averroes's achievements in law and medicine -- he was the first to describe the function of the retina -- as well as in philosophy made him a favourite in the court of Yaqub Al Mansour, the enlightened Khalif in Andalusian Spain.
The film, Chahine said, was a message of hope. "Maybe that's what irritates the obscurantists. They want to prove that joy does not belong in this world. Whereas I believe in it," he said..

Cairo-born, Canadian-raised director Atom Egoyan also confronts the extreme in his competition entry "The Sweet Hereafter", a gripping account of a small British Columbia town coping with a school bus accident which kills its children.

Ian Holm pulls off an impressive performance as the devil's advocate -- an ambulance-chasing lawyer seeking to reap the bitter harvest as anger and recrimination threaten to tear the small community apart.
Egoyan's previous Cannes competitor, "Exotica", won the International Critics' Prize in 1994 after bagging a host of Canadian Genie awards.
"The Sweet Hereafter" is based on a novel by Russell Banks, widely-seen as difficult to adapt because it takes the form of confessions by characters who each give their own account of events.
Asked if audiences would be able to confront such tragedy on film, Egoyan, 36, said: "That's what films are for. Confronting the most extreme things."
